summary: Defines a concise problem detail format for carrying machine-readable error information in REST responses for constrained environments. It is inspired by, but more compact than, the problem details format for HTTP APIs in RFC 7807, so APIs need not invent their own error formats. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: When a tiny device says no, it should say why in a short, standard way. This gives a compact error note that machines can read without custom formats.

subtitle: A compact CBOR format for machine-readable error details in CoAP responses.

tldr.problem: CoAP response codes often do not say enough about an error, and constrained devices cannot afford to define a new error format for every API.
tldr.mechanism: Concise Problem Details is a CBOR map with a few standard entries (title, detail, instance, response-code and others) plus extension slots, and it is sent as the body of an error response.
tldr.outcome: APIs can reuse one small error format. It is inspired by RFC 7807 problem details for HTTP APIs but is more concise, and an appendix covers carrying RFC 7807 data inside it.

today: RFC 9290 is a Proposed Standard from October 2022. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Problem Details for CoAP
sections.content:
REST response status information, such as CoAP response codes, is sometimes not enough to explain an error. This RFC defines a simple, extensible framework for CBOR data items that carry the finer-grained details. APIs can reuse it and define their own "shapes" of these items. Clients learn the high-level class of error from the response code and the details from the problem details.

The framework is largely inspired by the problem details for HTTP APIs in RFC 7807, but is meant to be more concise. Unlike RFC 7807 it has no explicit problem type: the category of the problem, called the "problem shape", is understood from which entries are present.
sections.eli5: A plain "no" is not very helpful. This lets a small device also hand over a short note saying what went wrong.

sections.title: The Basic Problem Details Map
sections.content:
A Concise Problem Details item is a CBOR map, described in CDDL. The standard entries use negative integer keys:

  • title (key -1): a short, human-readable summary of the problem shape.
  • detail (key -2): a human-readable explanation of this occurrence.
  • instance (key -3): a URI reference identifying this occurrence.
  • response-code (key -4): the CoAP response code.
  • base-uri (key -5): the base for resolving relative URIs in the item.
  • base-lang (key -6) and base-rtl (key -7): the language and writing direction of plain text strings.

The map must not be empty. Plain text without language information is read as language tag en and left-to-right direction.
sections.eli5: It is like a short error card with labeled blanks: a headline, a longer explanation, an ID for this particular problem, and a few more.

sections.title: How the Entries Behave
sections.content:
The title is advisory. The detail should help the client correct the problem rather than give server-side debugging information, and consumers SHOULD NOT parse it for information; extensions are a better way to carry such data.

The response-code is advisory too, but generators MUST use the same code as in the actual CoAP response, so that generic CoAP software that does not understand the format still behaves correctly. It helps when a message body is stored without its CoAP information or when an intermediary changed the code. The value is the numeric form of the code, so 4.04 Not Found is the number 132.

The base-uri is usually absent in the first request and response, since it can be inferred. Whoever stores the item may add it so that consumers can resolve relative URIs.
sections.eli5: The "detail" is for people, so programs should not try to read it. The response code in the note must match the real one, so simple devices are never confused.

sections.title: Standard and Custom Extensions
sections.content:
Extensions come in two kinds. Standard Problem Detail entries are generic and use negative integer keys in a global namespace, registered with IANA. Custom Problem Detail entries are application-specific and carry a nested map under a key that is either an unsigned integer or an absolute URI. Only the integer form needs registration. Integers are more compact; URIs need no registration and suit experimenting or tightly integrated environments. A URI key is for identification only and MUST NOT be dereferenced in the normal course of handling problem details.

Consumers MUST ignore standard or custom entries, or keys inside custom entries, that they do not recognize (the "ignore-unknown rule"), which lets the format evolve. When storing or forwarding an item, it is strongly RECOMMENDED to keep unrecognized entries. If an extension must change in a way where ignoring unknown parts would be unsafe, a new custom key can be registered.

The RFC also registers one more standard entry, unprocessed-coap-option (key -8), listing the numbers of CoAP options that the server could not process. It may be used to satisfy the "SHOULD" in Section 5.4.1 of RFC 7252.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to add your own notes: a short numbered label that must be registered, or a long name you make up yourself. Readers skip any label they do not know.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA created two subregistries in the Constrained RESTful Environments (CoRE) Parameters registry. "Standard Problem Detail Keys" uses the "Specification Required" procedure and starts with keys -1 to -8. "Custom Problem Detail Keys" uses "Expert Review" and starts with key 7807, named tunnel-7807. Names must match [a-z][-a-z0-9]*, and the designated expert is asked to give the shortest key values to registrations likely to be widely used.

The RFC also registers the media type application/concise-problem-details+cbor, the CoAP Content-Format ID 257 for it, and updates the reference for CBOR tag 38 to point to its Appendix A.
sections.eli5: A public list keeps everyone's labels from clashing, and the new note type gets its own official name and number.

sections.title: Language-Tagged Strings (Appendix A)
sections.content:
Appendix A is the archival documentation for CBOR tag 38. A language-tagged string is an array of length 2 or 3: a BCP 47 language tag as a UTF-8 text string, the text itself, and an optional direction. The direction is false for left-to-right, true for right-to-left, or null for automatic. If the third element is absent, context may supply the direction; with no context, the default is the same as null.

The examples include the English string "Hello" as 38(["en", "Hello"]) and a Hebrew string with direction true.
sections.eli5: This lets a text carry a sticker saying which language it is in and which way to read it, left to right or right to left.

sections.title: Interworking with RFC 7807
sections.content:
Appendix B defines custom entry 7807 (tunnel-7807) to carry an RFC 7807 problem details object inside a Concise Problem Details item. The JSON is first converted to CBOR. Its title, detail and instance move to the matching standard entries. Its type and status go to keys 0 and 1 of the custom entry, and all other members are moved there unchanged.

The reverse direction needs support from another document in progress, which the text says is planned to create an HTTP Problem Types Registry.
sections.eli5: If you already have an error note in the older web format, there is a recipe for repacking it into the compact format.

sections.title: Privacy and Security Considerations
sections.content:
Problem details can unintentionally disclose information, including Personally Identifiable Information. URIs inside them may be tracking vectors; some are not meant to be dereferenced, and even intended ones such as instance can leak information. Implementations should decide which component dereferences them and which servers are trusted.

The security and privacy considerations of RFC 7807 apply in full. Entities that store or forward these items need to consider whether information moves out of a context where access to it was acceptable. Sensitive information SHOULD NOT be obscured in ways, such as base64-encoding, that might make it look non-sensitive.
sections.eli5: An error note can accidentally give away secrets, so be careful what goes in it and where the copies end up.
